name: All-on-4
lead: All-on-4 is a prosthodontic treatment concept in which a full arch of missing teeth is replaced by a fixed prosthesis supported by four dental implants, the rear two usually tilted so they can be anchored without bone grafting. The prosthesis is typically fitted within about 24 hours of surgery, and "All-on-4" is a trademark of the implant manufacturer Nobel Biocare.[1] It is classed in looksmaxxing culture as a "hardmaxx" dental procedure because it is sometimes pursued to replace failing teeth with a new, uniform smile.

The concept was developed by the Portuguese prosthodontist Paulo Maló and colleagues and named in the early 2000s, building on earlier work on tilted and immediately loaded implants.[1][2] Published follow-up studies from Maló's group report high implant survival over several years, although much of the early research was funded by the manufacturer.[1][2]

This article records what is reported about the procedure. Entries in the ClinicalTrials.gov registry show that comparative trials of framework materials and implant configurations are ongoing, and no registered trial examined here was designed around facial appearance as an outcome.
infobox: Surgical and prosthetic full-arch implant procedure
About $30,000-$40,000 per arch, per one encyclopedia summary[1]

paras: The procedure replaces the teeth of an entire upper or lower arch, usually ten to fourteen, with a single fixed prosthesis attached to four implants. The two rear implants are angled so that they avoid the maxillary sinus in the upper jaw and the nerve canal in the lower jaw, which can allow treatment without grafting bone.[1][2]

A provisional prosthesis is typically attached on the day of surgery (immediate loading), and a definitive prosthesis is made later. Prosthetic teeth may be acrylic (PMMA) over a titanium bar or made of zirconia; the choice between the two is described as debated, with acrylic regarded as shock-absorbing and zirconia as more durable.[1] Planning commonly uses CBCT scans, and digital design and CAD-CAM manufacture are now common.[1][2]

Encyclopedia accounts trace the concept to Per-Ingvar Brånemark's osseointegration work from the 1960s and to later work on tilted posterior implants and immediate loading in the 1990s.[1][2] Maló is credited with a first patient in 1998 and a 2003 clinical study that named the approach "All-on-4"; Nobel Biocare commercialised it from about 2004.[2] One summary notes the view that the name was coined for an approach assembled from earlier techniques.[1] Nobel Biocare marked the concept's 25th anniversary in 2023, reporting more than 250,000 patients treated.[2]

Reported outcomes from the originating group include implant survival of about 98 percent at five years and about 95 percent at ten years in a mandibular cohort, with high prosthesis survival.[2] A 2013 systematic review and a 2019 long-term mandibular follow-up are cited in the Wikipedia article, which does not state their figures.[1] Much early research was sponsored by the manufacturer.[1]

ClinicalTrials.gov lists a number of small registered trials, mostly of prosthetic framework materials (PEEK versus cobalt-chromium or titanium) and marginal bone loss, and comparisons of All-on-4 with All-on-6 or zygomatic implants.[3][4][5][6][7] Registered enrolments are typically between 10 and 40 participants.

Acrylic prosthetic teeth on a titanium bar wear and need periodic replacement, and bone loss around implants may later require additional treatment.[1] Grokipedia reports long-term implant survival declining over 10 to 18 years in cohorts, with the figures drawn from the originating group.[2] As with other implant surgery, infection, bleeding and implant failure are recognised possibilities.

The procedure appears in lists of aesthetic dental options as a way to replace badly damaged or missing teeth with a complete, even set. Its high cost, reported at about 50 to 70 percent less in some countries according to a clinic-directory figure cited on Wikipedia, makes dental tourism a recurring topic.[1]

card.summary: Full-arch fixed teeth on four implants; established dental surgery with reported high survival, but pricey and aimed at tooth loss, not facial change.
card.note: Manufacturer-funded early research; prosthetic wear and bone loss reported.

quick.overview:
All-on-4 replaces a whole arch of teeth with a fixed bridge held by four implants, two of them angled to avoid grafting. Teeth are usually fitted within about a day of surgery.

In looksmaxxing circles it is discussed as a dental "hardmaxx" for people with failing or missing teeth. Long-term data come largely from the originating clinic and manufacturer-linked studies; independent trials are small.
quick.mechanism: Titanium implants fuse with the jaw bone. The tilted rear implants use denser front bone and avoid sinus and nerve areas, and a bridge screwed onto the implants is worn full-time.
quick.risks: Reported issues include wear of acrylic teeth, bone loss around implants, infection and implant failure. Costs are high and vary widely by country.
